title: Honor the book (Avot 4:6)
hook: Yose: whoever honors the Torah is honored
tomorrow: can anyone judge alone? Avot says only One can.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not a crown, not a spade: learning held for its own sake. Today, the last line of this stretch, and the week comes back.
screen: `NOT A CROWN, NOT A SPADE.` → `THE WEEK COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: In some Jewish homes, if a siddur or a Bible hits the floor, someone picks it up and kisses it before putting it back. Worn-out holy books aren't tossed in the recycling; traditionally they're buried, or set aside in a genizah. Rabbi Yose says why it matters: whoever honors the Torah is honored by people, and whoever disgraces the Torah is disgraced by people.
screen: `A BOOK HITS THE FLOOR.` → `PICKED UP AND KISSED.` → `HONORED BY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Notice the direction. Yose doesn't say honor the book and you'll be rewarded later. He says people see it, and it changes how they see you. The way you treat what you hold sacred is public, even when you think it isn't. A kiss on a dropped book is small. So is a hello said first, or a mouth kept shut in a group chat. That's the whole fortnight, really. Deep roots: the deeds below ground. Essentials first: the poor mother's birds before the clever math. One mitzvah brings another. Everyone has an hour. Very, very humble. Learn to do. Not a crown, not a spade. Each is a way of honoring the book: carrying it in your hands, not just your head. And the line runs the other way too: disgrace the Torah, and people see that as well. Honor isn't only a private feeling; it's something your hands do.
screen: `PEOPLE SEE IT.` · `SMALL ACTS OF HONOR.` · `A WEEK OF THEM.` · `IN THE HANDS, NOT THE HEAD.` · then, large: `HONOR THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Find a book near you that you value, sacred or not. Hold it in both hands, feel its weight and its cover, then set it down gently where it belongs. Let the rest of the sit be quiet, with it beside you.
Honor the book. Rabbi Yose's mechabed: whoever honors the Torah is honored by people.
Honor the book, and the honor comes back to you through people. Two weeks of Avot, carried well.
